Teacher Pack: IELTS Writing JURASSIC ENGLISH ™
3Licensed for one teacher / one centre. © Jurassic English
What you get in this pack
A complete IELTS Writing course for a class: ten 60-minute lessons with timings, projected text,
teacher notes, a class-mode line for every step, and the tools to mark without giving bands.
86 printable
A4
pages
This licensed PDF: the guide, ten lessons and the model scripts.
10 class
lessons
Six Task 2 lessons on the Thinking Cycle, then four Task 1 lessons (charts, tables, maps, processes and
letters).
1 marking
guide
Countable checks under the four IELTS Writing criteria, for Task 2 and Task 1.
24 margin
codes
Each code points to the lesson that ﬁxes it, so marking turns into the next lesson.
55 model
scripts
and
ﬁx-the-paragraph
keys
Band 6, 7 and 8-style models side by side, including full essays, reports and letters.
Every lesson, prompt, chart and model is written by Jurassic English; all data is invented. No exam-board or
published material is included. The marking guide paraphrases the four criteria and is not an oﬃcial band
scale. Models are illustrative and not oﬃcially rated.
Licence. One teacher or one centre. Class lessons for groups of 4–16 learners at Writing 5.0–6.0. Practice
material, not an oﬃcial score. No resale, sharing, uploading or redistribution. © 2026–2027 WorldWise
Learning and JurassicEnglish.com.

The Jurassic English Writing marking guide
Use this guide to mark and teach with. It is Jurassic English's own countable checklist, organised under the four
IELTS Writing criteria. It paraphrases what each criterion looks for and is not an oﬃcial band scale. Give
students the counts and the codes, not a band.

introduction
Project:
Prompt: Some people think that all university students should have a part-time job while they study. To what
extent do you agree or disagree?
Write the introduction only. 6 minutes. No help.
Teacher:
Start the 6:00 countdown. Say nothing. If the student asks a question, answer "Do your best; we will look
together."
At 6:00 say "Pens down." Use the last minute to take the paper.
In
class: Whole class, silent, on the projected countdown. Collect nothing yet.
Measure: Introduction written in 6:00, yes / no.

it

Self-assessment
Project:
Count your introduction:
Words: ____
Does one sentence say where you stand? yes / no
How many words copied in a row from the prompt? Longest run: ____
Does it say what the essay will do? yes / no
Teacher:
The student counts; you check the copying count with them by laying the prompt beside the text. A run of four
or more prompt words in the same order counts as copied.
Do not correct anything yet. Say: "This is your starting line."
In
class: Pairs swap papers and count each other's work with the card; the writer checks the partner's counts
and writes the ﬁnal numbers.
Measure: Words · position yes / no · longest copied run · map yes / no, written by the student.

1. Topic: what is it about? (2–4 words)
2. Task: what must I do? (agree? discuss? compare? solve?)

part: how many things must I answer?
Teacher:
Run them on Prompt A together. Key: topic: students working while they study · task: say how far you agree ·
parts: one (but note the word all: the question is about every student, which leaves room for a partial position).
Say: "The examiner's ﬁrst question about your essay is: did it answer this prompt, all of it?"
In
class: Teach to the whole class; take answers from three students before giving the key.
Measure: Three answers given for Prompt A.

Analyze
Project:
Match each instruction to its task.
a. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
b. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
c. Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?
d. What are the causes of this problem, and what can be done about it?
e. Why is this happening? Is it a positive or negative development?
f. Is this a good thing or a bad thing?
Tasks: 1 give your opinion · 2 present two views, then yours · 3 weigh good against bad and decide · 4 explain
causes and solutions · 5 answer two direct questions
Teacher:
Key: a–1 · b–2 · c–3 · d–4 · e–5 · f–1 (a single opinion question).
Teach: types 2, 3 and 5 each have two jobs. Missing one job is the most common Task 2 fault at this level.
In
class: Teach to the whole class; take answers from three students before giving the key.
Measure: Matched /6.

Project:
Prompt: Many people now move from the countryside to big cities to ﬁnd work. Why is this happening? What
problems does this cause for the countryside?
Underline each thing you must answer. How many parts? Write one word for each.
Teacher:
Key: two parts: (1) why people move (causes) · (2) problems for the countryside (not for the cities). The second
part is limited to the countryside: an essay about traﬃc in cities answers the wrong question.
